subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Fluid and Electrolyte Homeostasis: Holliday-Segar and Acid-Base

steps.tx: Daily maintenance water requirements in children correlate directly with physiological caloric expenditure rather than body weight alone. Under the classic **Holliday-Segar formula for maintenance fluids**, children require one hundred millilitres per kilogram for the first ten kilograms, fifty millilitres per kilogram for the second ten kilograms (eleven to twenty kilograms), and twenty millilitres per kilogram for each kilogram exceeding twenty kilograms.
steps.say: Calculate maintenance fluids using the Holliday-Segar rule: one hundred mL per kg for the first ten kilos, fifty for the next ten, and twenty for each kilo above twenty.

rows: Add 50 mL/kg/day for each kg over 10
Add 2 mL/kg/hour for each kg over 10
Add 20 mL/kg/day for each kg over 20
Add 1 mL/kg/hour for each kg over 20
Sodium: 2 to 3 mEq/kg/day; Potassium: 1 to 2 mEq/kg/day
Added after confirming adequate urine output

steps.tx: Contemporary pediatric fluid practice has shifted definitively away from historical hypotonic solutions to eliminate preventable iatrogenic morbidity. Modern international guidelines mandate utilizing **isotonic intravenous maintenance fluids** containing physiological sodium concentrations (such as 0.9% normal saline in five percent dextrose or Plasma-Lyte 148), because hospitalized children frequently secrete non-osmotic antidiuretic hormone, placing them at severe risk of fatal dilutional hyponatraemic encephalopathy.
steps.say: Use isotonic fluids like normal saline in five percent dextrose for maintenance. Hypotonic solutions cause fatal hospital-acquired hyponatremic encephalopathy due to ADH release.

left.title: Modern Practice: Isotonic Fluids
points: 0.9% normal saline + 5% dextrose (154 mEq/L Na)
Or balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte / Ringer lactate)
Completely prevents iatrogenic hospital hyponatraemia
Recommended standard of care in all pediatric guidelines

right.title: Obsolete Practice: Hypotonic Fluids
points: Historical 0.18% or 0.45% saline solutions
Excess free water rapidly enters brain cells
Non-osmotic ADH (pain, nausea, surgery) retains water
Provoked fatal cerebral edema, seizures, and herniation

steps.tx: Rapid shifts in extracellular sodium osmolality produce severe neurological injury secondary to cellular swelling or shrinkage. In acute symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures, emergency administration of **hypertonic three percent saline** (three to five millilitres per kilogram over ten to twenty minutes) rapidly raises serum sodium by three to five milliequivalents, aborting cerebral herniation. Conversely, chronic hyponatremia must not be corrected faster than ten to twelve milliequivalents per day.
steps.say: Treat symptomatic hyponatremic seizures with three to five mL per kg of three percent hypertonic saline. Correct chronic hyponatremia slowly to prevent osmotic demyelination.

left.title: Acute Symptomatic Hyponatraemia
points: Serum sodium drops acutely below 120-125 mEq/L
Presents with lethargy, vomiting, seizures, coma
Give 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 15 min)
Rapidly shrinks swollen brain astrocytes to stop herniation

right.title: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome Risk
points: Excessively rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia
Brain astrocytes cannot synthesize organic osmolytes quickly
Leads to central pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis
Strict correction speed limit: <10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours

steps.tx: Elevation of extracellular potassium concentration disrupts cardiac membrane potential, threatening lethal ventricular arrhythmias. The earliest electrocardiographic manifestation of **hyperkalaemia on electrocardiogram** is tall, symmetrical, narrow, peaked T waves, followed by PR interval prolongation, flattening of P waves, widening of the QRS complex into a sine-wave pattern, and fatal ventricular fibrillation or asystole as serum potassium exceeds 7.0 mEq/L.
steps.say: Hyperkalemia causes tall peaked T waves, followed by QRS widening and fatal sine-wave arrest. Intravenous calcium gluconate stabilizes cardiac membranes immediately.

vis.alt: Electrocardiogram rhythm strips displaying progressive stages of hyperkalemic toxicity from peaked T waves to sine-wave arrest.
vis.caption: Sequential electrocardiographic changes of hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity and immediate membrane stabilization protocols. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Immediate therapeutic management of severe hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity follows a clear sequential triad: stabilize, shift, and eliminate. Intravenous ten percent **calcium gluconate stabilizes myocardium** (0.5 mL/kg over five to ten minutes) by antagonizing the electrophysiological membrane depolarizing effect of potassium, followed by potassium-shifting therapies (insulin-dextrose infusion, salbutamol nebulization) and elimination via loop diuretics, potassium binders, or acute hemodialysis.
steps.say: Treat hyperkalemia with IV calcium gluconate for membrane stabilization, then shift potassium with insulin-dextrose or salbutamol, and eliminate with diuretics or dialysis.

rows: 10% Calcium gluconate (0.5 mL/kg IV over 5-10 min)
Beta-2 activation stimulates Na-K ATPase pump
Insulin drives potassium into cells with glucose
Renal excretion or gastrointestinal resin binding

steps.tx: Calculating the serum anion gap differentiates metabolic acidosis caused by unmeasured acid accumulation from bicarbonate-wasting disorders. Determining the **serum anion gap in metabolic acidosis** utilizing the formula: sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate (normal range eight to twelve milliequivalents per litre) divides acidosis into high anion gap acidosis (DKA, lactic acidosis, uremia, toxic ingestions) and normal anion gap acidosis (diarrhea, RTA).
steps.say: The serum anion gap is sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, normally eight to twelve. High gap indicates DKA, lactic acidosis, or toxins; normal gap indicates diarrhea or RTA.

rows: Loss of bicarbonate replaced by chloride (hyperchloraemic)
Severe acute diarrhoea, Renal tubular acidosis
Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Paraldehyde, Iron/INH, Lactic, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates
Systematic review of high anion gap toxins
Delta AG divided by Delta HCO3-

steps.tx: Systematic step-wise evaluation of arterial blood gas parameters identifies primary respiratory versus metabolic disorders and compensatory adequacy. Interpreting **arterial blood gas interpretation** begins by assessing pH (acidaemia <7.35, alkalaemia >7.45), followed by identifying primary directional changes in PaCO2 (respiratory) and HCO3- (metabolic), and verifying whether secondary compensatory changes fall within physiologically expected mathematical boundaries.
steps.say: Evaluate blood gases systematically: pH determines acidemia or alkalemia, PaCO2 reflects respiratory status, and bicarbonate indicates metabolic components.

left.title: Primary Acid-Base Disturbances
points: Metabolic acidosis: low pH, low HCO3-, compensatory low PaCO2
Metabolic alkalosis: high pH, high HCO3-, compensatory high PaCO2
Respiratory acidosis: low pH, high PaCO2, compensatory high HCO3-
Respiratory alkalosis: high pH, low PaCO2, compensatory low HCO3-

right.title: Winter Formula for Compensation
points: Expected PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis = (1.5 x HCO3-) + 8 +/- 2
If measured PaCO2 > expected: concurrent respiratory acidosis
If measured PaCO2 < expected: concurrent respiratory alkalosis
Detects complex mixed triple acid-base disturbances

steps.tx: Depression of ionized serum calcium concentration increases peripheral nerve and neuromuscular membrane excitability. Clinically manifesting with neuromuscular tetany, **pediatric acute hypocalcaemia** presents with perioral paresthesias, positive Chvostek sign (facial nerve tapping induces twitching of ipsilateral facial muscles), Trousseau sign (carpal spasm induced by inflating a sphygmomanometer cuff), laryngospasm causing stridor, and prolonged QTc interval on electrocardiogram.
steps.say: Hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular tetany with positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, laryngospasm, and prolonged QTc intervals. Treat with IV calcium gluconate.

rows: Tapping facial nerve anterior to tragus
Facial muscle twitching (angle of mouth / nose)
Inflate BP cuff >systolic pressure x 3 minutes
Carpal spasm: flexion of wrist & MCP joints
More specific than Chvostek for hypocalcaemia
Delayed myocardial repolarization from low calcium
Dilute in 5% dextrose; monitor heart rate

steps.tx: A cuff blown above systolic pressure and left for three minutes can draw the thumb across the palm and extend the fingers at the interphalangeal joints. That posture is **main d'accoucheur**, and provoking it is the Trousseau sign of latent tetany from a low ionised calcium. Tapping the facial nerve, the Chvostek sign, is the other bedside test. The QT interval may lengthen. In a child the urgent risk is laryngospasm, so the airway is watched while calcium is replaced.
steps.say: Inflating a blood pressure cuff for three minutes produces carpal spasm, the Trousseau sign, when ionised calcium is low. The thumb adducts across the palm. Laryngospasm is the risk in a child.

vis.alt: Positive Trousseau sign, with carpal spasm while a blood pressure cuff is inflated.
vis.caption: With the cuff inflated, the hand goes into carpal spasm and the thumb is drawn across the palm. Illustration: StewardMD original.
